content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh is the meat from the upper leg of a chicken with the skin removed. It is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as iron and zinc. The thigh remains juicy even without skin, making it a popular choice for a variety of cooking methods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more fat than breast meat, but removing the skin dramatically reduces the fat content.
The meat of the thigh is considered more flavorful due to a higher concentration of intramuscular fat.
In many traditional cuisines (e.g., Russian, French, Japanese) skinless thighs are commonly used for braising and roasting.
Thighs can be grilled, baked, pan‑seared, or cooked in a slow cooker while staying moist without added fats.
Athletes often choose skinless thighs for muscle‑building diets because of their high protein content.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Skinless chicken thigh provides about 20‑25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin (B3), which are important for metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: A source of iron, zinc, and selenium, nutrients that support immunity and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Practically carbohydrate‑free, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and moderate fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Chicken can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; ensure thorough cooking to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Even without skin, thighs contain some fat; those monitoring fat intake should account for the calories.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Hormones and antibiotics
items.content: When purchasing, look for certifications confirming the meat is free from unwanted additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless thighs can be baked, pan‑seared, grilled, or cooked in a slow cooker. Season with salt, pepper, herbs (rosemary, thyme) or your favorite spices. For baking, preheat to 180 °C and cook 25‑30 minutes until golden and fully cooked.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen thighs in the refrigerator before use.

chow-mein-or-chop-suey-ns-as-to-type-of-.title: Chow Mein or Chop Suey (no noodles)

content.title: About
content.content: Chow mein and chop suey are popular Chinese‑style stir‑fry dishes featuring meat (commonly beef, chicken or pork), vegetables and a savory soy‑based sauce. This version omits noodles, focusing on the protein, crisp veggies and aromatic sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Both dishes are traditionally cooked quickly over high heat in a wok to retain vegetable crunch.
Classic chow mein uses egg noodles and chop suey often includes rice, but both can be made noodle‑free.
The sauce typically combines soy sauce, oyster sauce, ginger and garlic.
In the United States chop suey is frequently served as a meat‑and‑veggie mix without noodles, making it a low‑carb option.
Garnishes often include sliced green onion and toasted sesame seeds.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: Omitting noodles makes the dish suitable for low‑carb or ketogenic diets.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Vegetables such as bell pepper, carrot and broccoli add vitamin C, vitamin A and potassium.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Ginger and garlic contain antioxidant compounds that support immune function.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Oyster sauce and spices may help boost metabolic rate.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy and oyster sauces are high in salt; people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to soy should avoid the sauce or use a suitable substitute.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Undercooked or improperly handled meat can harbor pathogens.

items.title: High‑heat cooking
items.content: Stir‑frying at very high temperatures can produce small amounts of acrylamide; avoid over‑cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté sliced meat in a hot wok until browned, add vegetables and stir‑fry for 3‑5 minutes. Pour a mixture of soy sauce, oyster sauce, ginger and garlic, toss to coat evenly. Serve hot, garnished with green onions and toasted sesame seeds.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 1 month after cooling completely.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce, Seafood and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: This is a home recipe for whole‑grain pasta tossed with a tomato‑based sauce, seafood (shrimp, mussels, calamari) and added vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, spinach). The dish is rich in fiber, protein and healthy fats, while the tomato sauce provides lycopene and the seafood adds omega‑3 fatty acids.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta retains bran and germ, boosting B‑vitamins and mineral content.
Fresh‑tomato sauce contains more lycopene when gently heated.
Seafood is one of the best natural sources of iodine, essential for thyroid function.
Spinach adds iron and folate to the meal.
Such combinations are traditional in Mediterranean cuisine, where pasta, tomatoes and seafood are prized together.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supports regular digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Seafood provides EPA and DHA, which benefit heart and brain health.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Bell pepper and spinach add vitamin C, vitamin K and iron.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta leads to more stable blood‑sugar levels compared with refined pasta.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to shrimp, mussels or calamari.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce can be salty; monitor added salt to keep sodium intake moderate.

items.title: Food interactions
items.content: Large portions of seafood may enhance the effects of certain medications, such as anticoagulants.

items.title: Digestive load
items.content: The combination of fiber and protein can be heavy for sensitive stomachs; consume in moderate portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and seafood. Finish with fresh basil or a sprinkle of Parmesan cheese, and optionally garnish with lemon wedges.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked pasta in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Keep dry whole‑grain pasta in a cool, dry place in a sealed package for up to 12 months.
